subject: Banking
title: Due Diligence Deep Dives
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Due Diligence Deep Dives.

hook.text: Before closing a deal, buyers investigate every detail of the target company.

buildup.text: Teams review finances, contracts, lawsuits, IP, employee agreements, and tax liabilities. Every closet gets opened.

discovery.text: Virtual data rooms replaced physical ones. Thousands of documents are uploaded to secure platforms for buyer review.

twist.text: HP bought Autonomy for $11 billion in 2011 then wrote off $8.8 billion. Due diligence missed massive accounting fraud.

climax.text: Due diligence is the buyer's last line of defense. When it fails, billions can vanish on day one of ownership.

punchline.text: $8.8 billion lost from missed fraud. Due diligence saves or sinks deals.

quiz.question: What happened when HP's due diligence on Autonomy failed?
options: HP lost $8.8 billion from undiscovered accounting fraud

details.summary: Due diligence is the exhaustive investigation that investment banks and acquirers conduct before completing a deal, reviewing financial statements, legal liabilities, contracts, intellectual property, and operational risks.
details.whyItMatters: Due diligence protects buyers from overpaying or inheriting hidden liabilities. Shortcuts in due diligence have resulted in some of history's worst acquisitions, destroying billions in shareholder value.
takeaways: Financial, legal, operational, and tax due diligence are all conducted
Data rooms contain thousands of documents for buyers to review
Junior bankers and lawyers spend weeks analyzing every detail

faq.question: What happens in a due diligence data room?
faq.answer: The target company uploads thousands of documents including financial statements, contracts, employee records, legal disputes, and intellectual property filings. Buyers' teams review everything to identify risks, liabilities, and verify claimed performance.

faq.question: What is the biggest due diligence failure in history?
faq.answer: Hewlett-Packard's acquisition of Autonomy for 11 billion dollars in 2011. HP later wrote off 8.8 billion, alleging that Autonomy had inflated revenues through accounting fraud that due diligence failed to catch.
